title: End-to-end browser navigation and web request lifecycle
concepts: A URL navigation crosses browser, operating system, resolver, network, TLS endpoint, HTTP infrastructure, application middleware, data dependencies, and renderer boundaries; many requests skip work because of caches or reused connections.
DNS resolution, address selection, TCP or QUIC transport setup, TLS authentication, and HTTP negotiation are related but distinct stages whose order and reuse vary by protocol and connection state.
HTTP defines request/response semantics; proxies, CDNs, load balancers, server middleware, and application handlers can transform, route, authorize, cache, or reject the exchange.

Browser security policies such as same-origin, CORS, cookie rules, CSP, and mixed-content checks affect whether requests are sent, credentials are attached, and responses are exposed to script; they are not substitutes for server authorization.
HTTP caching, service-worker CacheStorage, browser memory caches, and application data stores have different owners and freshness rules; diagnose which layer served the response.

After HTML arrives, the browser parses and discovers resources, builds render-related structures, runs scripts, computes styles/layout, paints, and may hydrate or update a React tree; critical rendering and interactivity are affected by resource dependencies.

Performance and production debugging require timelines and evidence at each boundary, including cache state, DNS/connect/TLS timing, redirects, server spans, response size, main-thread work, and rendering milestones.

practiceProblems.name: Trace a slow product-page navigation
practiceProblems.statement: A React product page feels slow. Browser records show a redirect, DNS/connect time, a large JavaScript bundle, an API request, and delayed LCP. Build a step-by-step investigation plan that separates network, server, and rendering costs.
constraints: Do not assume every navigation performs fresh DNS, TCP, and TLS setup.
The endpoint may return quickly while client rendering remains slow.
Some browser console errors describe response exposure rather than whether a network request reached the server.

examples.input: Warm navigation, cached assets, API response in 120 ms, LCP in 3.8 s
examples.output: Compare cold and warm waterfalls, inspect redirect/resource dependencies and long tasks, and optimize the measured critical path rather than the already-fast API alone.

practiceProblems.name: Diagnose a cross-origin API request failure
practiceProblems.statement: A React app calls an ASP.NET Core API on another origin. The browser reports a CORS error after a preflight; the developer suspects the bearer token is invalid. Diagnose the request and propose a safe correction.
constraints: CORS is enforced by browsers and does not authorize access to server data.
Credentialed requests require a specific allowed origin, not a wildcard.
A preflight may be rejected before the actual request is sent.

examples.input: OPTIONS receives 401 and no actual POST appears in server logs
examples.output: Inspect middleware/proxy handling for OPTIONS and the required CORS policy before debugging POST authorization; then verify credentials and authorization on the actual request.

comparisons: Navigation versus subresource fetch: browser-controlled document transition versus script-initiated request and response exposure.
TCP plus TLS versus QUIC: distinct transport setup paths; HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 do not mean the same transport.
CORS versus authentication/authorization: browser response-sharing policy versus server access-control decision.
HTTP cache versus CacheStorage: protocol freshness semantics versus application-managed request/response entries.
Server latency versus page readiness: response completion and browser render/interactivity milestones measure different user experiences.

sourceSnapshot.authority: WHATWG Fetch and HTML standards; IETF DNS/TLS/HTTP/QUIC standards; MDN browser guides; Microsoft ASP.NET Core documentation; web.dev performance guidance
sourceSnapshot.edition: Current standards and official documentation checked 2026-11-21; runtime and browser behavior may vary by protocol negotiation and deployment.

accuracyFacts: A navigation may reuse DNS answers, connections, cached resources, or a service-worker response; do not describe every request as a fresh full handshake.
CORS controls whether browser script may access a cross-origin response; it is not server-side authentication or authorization.
A failed preflight can prevent the actual request from being sent; a browser CORS error alone does not prove the server never received any request.
HTTP/2 commonly uses a TCP connection with TLS for HTTPS; HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP. Negotiated protocol and setup details depend on browser and server support.
Server response latency, LCP, and INP measure different parts of the user experience and cannot be substituted for one another.
Cache-Control applies to HTTP caching semantics; CacheStorage behavior is controlled by application code.
Forwarded headers are trustworthy only when accepted from known proxies; client-supplied forwarding headers are untrusted input.
React hydration expects the client initial output to match server-rendered markup; browser-only state should not silently change the initial tree.
scopeExclusions: Exhaustive DNS, TLS, HTTP, Fetch, cookie, React DOM, or ASP.NET Core API inventories; their dedicated topics remain authoritative for exact APIs.
Provider-specific router, CDN, load-balancer, and operating-system configuration beyond the generic request path.
A claim that every browser navigation follows one fixed sequence; caches, preconnect, service workers, protocol negotiation, and browser implementation change the path.
